name: Kua'nsi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Huang, Huade. 2024. A Grammar of Kua'nsi. PhD thesis, The Australian National University, Canberra. xxii+523 pp. hdl:1885/316664 (open access, ANU Open Research; thesis submitted August 2023).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.4 Tone and 2.4.1 Tonal inventory, pp. 46-47; section 3.1.1 Phonological word, pp. 52-53.
catalog_quote: As defined, Kua’nsi is a tonal language. It uses tones primarily to distinguish lexical meaning. The indication of grammatical function is only a marginal function of tone in Kua’nsi. [...] Kua’nsi primarily distinguishes three lexical tones, low-falling /21/, mid-level /33/, and high-level /55/. There is one marginal lexical tone, low-rising /13/ that only occurs with the augmentative particle /lwa¹³~dwa¹³/. [...] In Kua’nsi, although tones are usually associated with vowels, the TBU is not the vowel but the syllable. [...] These lexical tones are assigned to every syllable in the lexicon, and there are no toneless syllables. [p. 52] The Kua’nsi phonological word can be defined by the three prosodic and segmental criteria: possible pause, possible lengthening of final vowel and glottal stop in word-initial onset. [...] Vowel length is not a phonological contrast in Kua’nsi, and non-final syllables do not show a significant difference in terms of duration. Lengthening usually occurs at the final syllable of a phonological word, typically when speakers are thinking while speaking, listing different items or finishing up the speech.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kua'nsi is described as a syllable-tone language: every syllable carries one of three lexical tones (21, 33, 55; marginal 13), there are no toneless/reduced syllables, and the phonological word is delimited by pause, optional lengthening of the word-final vowel and word-initial glottal onsets. The grammar makes no statement about word stress or accent at all; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Prosodic remarks limited to: word-final vowels may be lengthened in discourse (a boundary cue, 'always on the final syllable of a word'); reduplicated initial syllables bearing derived tone /13/ are longer than their base; polar questions are not intonationally marked.
new_statements.domain_note: Description based on a spontaneous-speech corpus from Liuhe Town, Heqing County; tone is lexical per syllable; final-vowel lengthening is explicitly a phonological-word/phrase boundary phenomenon, not described as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe Kua-nsi/Kua'nsi of Liuhe Town (Hedong, San'gezhuang etc.), Heqing County, Dali Prefecture = Glottolog kuan1249, ISO ykn. Castro et al. 2010 found Kua-nsi internally homogeneous; the related Heqing varieties Kuamasi (yku), Zibusi, Laizisi and Sonaga are separate languages and are not covered by the quoted statement.
